title: 2 Chronicles 2:1–10
context: Solomon decides to build a house for the LORD’s name and a house for his kingdom, counts a large labor force, and writes to Huram king of Tyre for a skilled craftsman and for timber from Lebanon, offering provisions in return. WEB spellings are followed here: the Tyrian king is Huram, not Hiram as in 1 Kings 5. In the common English and Hebrew alignment, WEB 2:1 is numbered as 1:18 in the Hebrew chapter division, so the rest of this chapter in WEB runs one verse ahead of the Hebrew numbering. The notes keep the WEB numbers and mention that shift only as a numbering fact, not as a change in the text itself. The unit is the Chronicler’s counterpart to 1 Kings 5:1–12, already drafted in this worktree, and should be read beside that letter without forcing the two into one form. Labor figures in 2:2, seventy thousand bearers, eighty thousand stone cutters, and three thousand six hundred overseers, match 2:18 and differ from 1 Kings 5:15–16, which has the same bearer and cutter counts but “three thousand three hundred” chief officers. 1 Kings 5:13 also records a levy of thirty thousand from all Israel that this chapter does not state in the same way. The provisions in 2:10, twenty thousand cors of beaten wheat and twenty thousand baths each of barley, wine, and oil for the timber cutters, differ from 1 Kings 5:11, which names twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of pure oil for Hiram’s household year by year. The already drafted 1 Kings 5 notes treat those figures as a difference interpreters explain in different ways, not as a doctrinal issue. Both traditions read the letter as Solomon’s real request for help to build the LORD’s house, and they do not invent a party contrast over the numbers or the names.

verses.text: Now Solomon decided to build a house for the LORD’s name, and a house for his kingdom.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Now Solomon decided to build a house for the LORD’s name, and a house for his kingdom.” The verse states the two buildings at the head of the chapter.

Arminian readers take the decision as a real resolve at the start of the work, a house for the LORD’s name and a royal house beside it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from the stated purpose. The house is for the LORD’s name, and a house for the kingdom is named with it, as Huram will later repeat.

Both traditions read the verse as Solomon’s decision to begin the work, without a party contrast over the two houses.

verses.text: Solomon counted out seventy thousand men to bear burdens, eighty thousand men who were stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred to oversee them.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon counts “seventy thousand men to bear burdens, eighty thousand men who were stone cutters in the mountains, and three thousand six hundred to oversee them.” The same three figures return in 2:18. 1 Kings 5:15–16 has seventy thousand who bore burdens and eighty thousand stone cutters, but “three thousand three hundred” chief officers over the work. The already drafted 1 Kings 5:16 notes record that difference and treat it as a question of counting, not as a theological issue.

Arminian readers name both overseer totals and refuse to hide one figure by the other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stay consistent with those Kings notes. Three thousand six hundred stands here; three thousand three hundred stands in 1 Kings 5:16. The bearer and cutter counts agree.

Both traditions leave the overseer figures unharmonized and invent no doctrine from the numbers.

verses.text: Solomon sent to Huram the king of Tyre, saying, “As you dealt with David my father, and sent him cedars to build him a house in which to dwell, so deal with me.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon sends to “Huram the king of Tyre,” asking, “As you dealt with David my father, and sent him cedars to build him a house in which to dwell, so deal with me.” WEB uses Huram here for the king 1 Kings 5 calls Hiram. The request appeals to the earlier help given to David. 1 Kings 5:2–6 is a longer letter, with other reasons David did not build; this opening is shorter and should be left as it is.

Arminian readers hear a real diplomatic appeal, grounded in a past dealing, not a form letter imported from Kings.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the WEB spelling and the shorter form. Huram is asked to deal with Solomon as he had dealt with David, sending cedars for a house.

Both traditions name the 1 Kings 5 parallel without rewriting this greeting from the other book.

verses.text: Behold, I am about to build a house for the name of the LORD my God, to dedicate it to him, to burn before him incense of sweet spices, for the continual show bread, and for the burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths, on the new moons, and on the set feasts of the LORD our God. This is an ordinance forever to Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
He is about to build “a house for the name of the LORD my God,” to dedicate it, to burn incense of sweet spices, for the continual show bread, and for the burnt offerings morning and evening, on the Sabbaths, the new moons, and the set feasts. “This is an ordinance forever to Israel.” The letter names the house’s worship uses more fully than the matching request in 1 Kings 5.

Arminian readers take the list as the actual purpose of the house: incense, show bread, and the regular offerings of Israel’s calendar.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also hear a house built for the LORD’s name and for the ordained worship of Israel, an ordinance said to be forever.

Both traditions read the verse as Solomon’s stated reason for building, not as a type to be pressed beyond the text.

verses.text: “The house which I am building will be great, for our God is greater than all gods.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The house which I am building will be great, for our God is greater than all gods.” The greatness of the house is tied to the greatness of God, not to Solomon’s fame. The claim is the ground for asking Tyre’s help, and it will be balanced in the next verse by the confession that no house can contain him.

Arminian readers hear a confession offered in a real letter: the house is great because God is greater than all gods.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same confession. Greatness belongs first to God; the house is great only as a house for his name.

Both traditions take the verse as shared praise, not as a party argument about the nations’ gods.

verses.text: But who is able to build him a house, since heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain him? Who am I then, that I should build him a house, except just to burn incense before him?
verses.arminianNotes:
“But who is able to build him a house, since heaven and the heaven of heavens can’t contain him? Who am I then, that I should build him a house, except just to burn incense before him?” The builder himself denies that a house can hold God. The work is limited: a place to burn incense before him. The thought is close to the later temple prayer, and it already guards the project against any claim that God is confined there.

Arminian readers hear a sincere limit on the building. Solomon does not think the house will contain God.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also start from God’s immensity. Heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain him, so the house is for worship, not for housing him.

Both traditions take the confession as shared ground, a check on any reading that would turn the measurements later in chapter 3 into a map of God’s being.

verses.text: “Now therefore send me a man skillful to work in gold, in silver, in bronze, in iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue, and who knows how to engrave engravings, to be with the skillful men who are with me in Judah and in Jerusalem, whom David my father provided.
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon asks for “a man skillful to work in gold, in silver, in bronze, in iron, and in purple, crimson, and blue, and who knows how to engrave engravings,” to work with the skillful men David has already provided in Judah and Jerusalem. 1 Kings 5 emphasizes timber and labor in this correspondence; the named craftsman in 1 Kings 7:13–14 appears later. This letter already asks for such a man.

Arminian readers take the request as a practical need. The work requires skill Solomon’s court does not claim to have alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also read a real request for a craftsman, to stand with those David provided. The later identification of Huram-abi belongs to the reply in 2:13–14.

Both traditions leave the two books’ timing and detail side by side, without forcing this verse to match the later scene in 1 Kings 7.

verses.text: “Send me also cedar trees, cypress trees, and algum trees out of Lebanon, for I know that your servants know how to cut timber in Lebanon. Behold, my servants will be with your servants,
verses.arminianNotes:
He also asks for “cedar trees, cypress trees, and algum trees out of Lebanon,” because Huram’s servants know how to cut timber there, and he offers his own servants to work with them. 1 Kings 5:6 asks for cedars from Lebanon in a similar way. Algum trees are named here; the exact wood is left as the text gives it, without a confident botanical claim the verse does not make.

Arminian readers hear a joint labor plan, servants of both kings at work in Lebanon.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name the trees as the letter names them and keep the parallel with 1 Kings 5:6, without merging the wording.

Both traditions take the request as a timber contract, not as a symbol of the nations.

verses.text: even to prepare timber in abundance for me; for the house which I am about to build will be great and wonderful.
verses.arminianNotes:
The timber is needed in abundance, “for the house which I am about to build will be great and wonderful.” The request is scaled to the house already called great in 2:5. The verse explains the quantity, not a hidden meaning in the wood.

Arminian readers take the abundance as a practical need for a large building, stated in the letter itself.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise refuse to allegorize the timber or the house’s greatness. The letter asks for much wood because the house will be great and wonderful.

Both traditions keep the verse in the register of a building request.

verses.text: Behold, I will give to your servants, the cutters who cut timber, twenty thousand cors of beaten wheat, twenty thousand baths of barley, twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Solomon will give the cutters “twenty thousand cors of beaten wheat, twenty thousand baths of barley, twenty thousand baths of wine, and twenty thousand baths of oil.” 1 Kings 5:11 records twenty thousand cors of wheat and twenty cors of pure oil for Hiram’s household, year by year, a different list and different quantities. The already drafted 1 Kings 5:11 notes name this verse and say interpreters explain the difference in different ways.

Arminian readers report both lists and do not invent a single reconstructed ration as if the two verses had said the same thing.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stay consistent with those Kings notes. The goods and the amounts are not identical, and the difference is not a doctrinal issue.

Both traditions leave the figures unharmonized and close the letter as a real offer of provisions for the work.
